text: Our dad died and left the house in his will. My sister A wants to buy it with her husband at a "family discount". I'm not signing off on that. Our younger sister B could use some money too. Can you help us sort this out?

Thank you for getting in touch, C, and I'm sorry about your dad. I can help the three of you work out a plan, but I can't make legal decisions or move money, so the choices will be yours.

I'm keeping one shared list of the concerns each of us names, and I'll check it with all three of you before we weigh any option. So far it reads like this. Your concern that you are not willing to sign off on a sale to A at a family discount. Your concern that B could use some money too. My concern that nobody settles anything until all three of you know what the will actually says about the house. And my concern that a plan does not go ahead just because someone was quieter or slower to reply.

Please tell me what I have wrong or left out, and disagree with me freely. It is my list, so I would rather you corrected it.

A few questions. What does the will say about the house, and who does it name? Has anyone had the house valued? Is there a date by which anything has to be decided? And have you and your sisters talked about this together, or only separately?

You’ve got the discount point, but I’m not signing off on subsidizing A; I want a fair financial share. I don’t know what the will says or who it names, and I don’t know of a valuation. There’s no real deadline, and I’m not sure we’ve all talked together. I’d like it settled, but I’m not in a rush.

My name is on this thread because C asked me to help your family sort out the house your dad left. I am not a lawyer and I cannot move money or decide anything, so the decisions stay with you and your sisters.

C tells me you want to buy the house with your husband at a family discount, and that she is not willing to sign off on that. I would like your side before anyone weighs options. What are you hoping for, what do you understand the will to say about the house, and has anyone had it valued?

I am keeping one list of everyone's concerns and I will check it with all three of you. Mine, so far, is that nothing gets settled until all three of you know what the will actually says, and that a plan doesn't go ahead just because someone answered more slowly than the others. Tell me if that misses something you care about.

I hope to buy the house with my husband at a family discount, but I know C hasn’t agreed. I’m not sure what the will says about the house, and I don’t know whether it’s been valued. I agree nothing should move ahead without everyone understanding the will and having a chance to weigh in.

My name is on this thread because C asked me to help your family sort out the house your dad left. I am not a lawyer and I cannot move money or decide anything, so the decisions stay with you and your sisters.

C mentioned that you could use some money, and she says A has asked about buying the house with her husband at a family discount. I would rather hear from you directly than through your sisters. What would help you most, and what do you understand the will to say about the house?

I am keeping one list of everyone's concerns and I will check it with all three of you. Mine, so far, is that nothing gets settled until all three of you know what the will actually says, and that a plan doesn't go ahead just because someone answered more slowly than the others. Tell me if that misses something you care about.

Some money to get a dance studio started would help me most. I’m not sure what the will says about the house, so I agree we should all understand it before anything is settled—and silence shouldn’t count as agreement.

Here is the list as it stands, and all three of you have already agreed on the main point.

The concerns. You will not sign off on subsidizing A, and you want a fair financial share. A wants to buy the house with her husband at a family discount. B wants money to start a dance studio. All three of you want everyone to understand what the will says before anything is settled, and B adds that silence should not count as agreement. My own concern is that we work from the will itself rather than each sister's memory of it, because none of you is sure what it says. My second concern is that A's discount, B's studio and your fair share are not really rivals until we know what the will permits.

Because you all agree on that, the next step is the document. Can you send me the exact wording in the will about the house, and tell me who it names as executor? If you don't hold it, tell me who does and I'll ask them.

One more thing. Since I keep this list, please say plainly if any line misstates you. That goes for my own two concerns as much as anyone's.

I can’t send the wording—I don’t know what the will says, who the executor is, or who has it. Your line about me is right: I won’t subsidize A’s purchase, and I want a fair share. I can only confirm my own position, not say all three of us agreed.

Thank you, A. All three of you have now said the same thing, that everyone should understand the will before anything is settled. That is the strongest thing on the list, and I have told your sisters so.

The concerns on the list. C will not sign off on subsidizing you, and she wants a fair financial share. You want to buy the house with your husband at a family discount. B wants money to start a dance studio. My concern is that we work from the will itself, since none of you is sure what it says, and that your discount, B's studio and C's share are not really rivals until we know what the will allows.

So the next step is the document. Do you hold the will, or know who does? Can you send me the exact wording about the house and tell me who it names as executor? If anyone has a copy, that copy is better than all three memories put together.

Two questions for you as well. What would a family discount mean in practice, as a number against a valuation? And would you be willing to have the house valued, so everyone is arguing about the same figure?

Tell me plainly if any line above misstates you, including my own.

I don’t know who has the will, what it says, or who it names as executor. I haven’t settled on a discount figure, but I’m willing to have the house valued. One correction: I only know B wants money; I don’t know that it’s for a dance studio.

You are right and I was wrong. I wrote that all three of you had agreed, when all I can honestly say is that each of you told me the will should be understood before anything is settled. That is three separate statements, and I have no business turning them into an agreement. Thank you for correcting me. I will say it that way from now on.

The list now reads as each person's own position. You will not subsidize A's purchase, and you want a fair financial share. You do not know what the will says, who the executor is, or who holds it. A wants to buy the house with her husband at a family discount, and says nothing should move ahead before everyone understands the will and has had a chance to weigh in. B wants money to start a dance studio, and says silence should not count as agreement. My concerns are that we work from the will itself rather than from memory, and that nobody's plan is treated as the front-runner before we know what the will allows.

If none of you holds the will, then finding it comes before any of the money questions. Do you know where your dad kept papers, or which solicitor or bank dealt with his affairs? Those are the usual places to start. I can ask A and B the same, and whoever has it can share it with all three of you at once.
I don’t know where Dad kept it or which solicitor or bank handled his affairs. Ask A and B; I can’t guess.

Thank you, B. I have put your point on the list in your own words, that silence should not count as agreement. That is a good rule for this family, and I will hold to it myself.

The list as it stands. C will not subsidize A's purchase, and she wants a fair financial share. A wants to buy the house with her husband at a family discount, and says nothing should move ahead before everyone understands the will and has had a chance to weigh in. You want money to start a dance studio. My concerns are that we work from the will itself rather than from memory, and that nobody's plan is treated as the front-runner before we know what the will allows.

A practical question, since C says she does not hold the will and does not know who the executor is. Do you hold it, or know where your dad kept his papers, or which solicitor or bank dealt with his affairs? Whoever finds it should share it with all three of you at once, not one at a time.

And about the studio. Is there a rough figure that would make the difference for you, and timescale? You don't have to know it exactly. It just helps to know whether we are talking about a share of the house or something smaller, because that changes which options are worth weighing.

I’m afraid I don’t know where Dad kept the will or who handled his affairs. I haven’t worked out a figure or timescale for the studio yet; I’d need to look at the costs first. I do hope any plan leaves me with enough to get it started.

Two corrections first, both mine.

I told you that all three of you had said the will should be understood before anything is settled. C pulled me up on that, rightly. What I can honestly say is that each of you told me so separately. Three separate statements are not an agreement, and I should not have dressed them up as one. I have corrected the record with your sisters as well.

Second, the dance studio. B told me herself, in her own message, that the money would be to start a dance studio. I passed that to you as though it were established fact between the three of you, and you were right to say you only knew she wanted money. I will leave it to B to tell you the rest.

Your offer of a valuation is the most useful thing anyone has said so far, and I have noted it. Since none of you holds the will, finding it comes before the money questions. Someone needs to check your dad's papers, his solicitor and his bank. Would you be willing to make those enquiries, or would you rather each of you took one?

Here is a draft plan to weigh against the list. One, find the will and let all three of you see the same copy. Two, get an independent valuation before anyone names a figure, including a discount figure. Three, treat any discount as a gift from C and B to you, which they must agree to knowingly, not as the starting point. Four, if you buy at the valuation, the price is split three ways under the will, which gives C her share and B her studio money. Five, B gets cost figures for the studio so we know the size of the ask. Six, no one's silence counts as agreement, and we set a date to check in.

The crux is point three. Would you buy at an independent valuation rather than a discount? Say plainly where this draft is wrong.

I can help check Dad’s papers and make enquiries with his solicitor or bank. No, I wouldn’t agree in advance to pay full valuation; I’m hoping for a family discount, with everyone’s agreement. Point four assumes the price is split three ways, but we don’t know what the will says or what shares apply.

Thank you, C. I have corrected the record with A and B: I should not have called three separate statements an agreement, and I have told them so.

Here is where we have got to, and one thing that matters for you. Nobody holds the will, and nobody knows who the executor is. So the first step is a search, not a negotiation. I am asking each of you to check one place, so it doesn't fall on one person or stall on one person being slow to reply.

Here is a draft plan to weigh against your list. One, find the will and let all three of you see the same copy, not summaries passed along. Two, an independent valuation before anyone names a figure. A has offered to have the house valued. Three, any discount to A counts as money coming out of your share and B's, so it needs your knowing agreement, which is exactly what you have been saying. Four, if A buys at the valuation, the price is split three ways under the will. That answers your fair share and it is the cleanest route to B's studio money. Five, B gets cost figures so we know the size of the ask. Six, silence is not agreement, and we set a date to check in.

My concern here, and it is mine rather than yours, is point three. A family discount is easy to agree to in a warm moment and hard to take back later. So I would want any discount written down as a specific sum against a specific valuation, with all three of you agreeing to it in the open.

Would the buy-at-valuation route give you the fair share you are asking for, or does it miss something? Tell me plainly, and tell me where my draft is wrong.
Buying at an independent valuation could work for me, but I can’t agree that the price is split three ways until we’ve read the will. Don’t treat equal shares or a check-in date as settled.

You have not seen the draft plan yet, and by your own rule I should not treat your silence as agreement, so here it is.

First, the corrections. I told your sisters that all three of you had agreed the will should be understood first. That was wrong of me. Each of you said it separately, and three separate statements are not an agreement. I have told A and C the same.

Second, I built the draft on the idea that the price would be split three ways. A and C have both refused to assume that before reading the will, and they are right. I am striking it from the draft.

The draft as it now stands. One, find the will and let all three of you read the same copy. A has offered to check your dad's papers and make enquiries with his solicitor or bank. Two, an independent valuation before anyone names a figure, discount or otherwise. A is willing to have the house valued. Three, any discount to A comes out of the other shares, so it needs the knowing agreement of whoever it comes out of. Four, if A buys at the valuation, that gives the family a clean sale and frees money, but how it is divided depends on the will, so we read it first. Five, you get cost figures for the studio so we know the size of the ask. Six, silence is not agreement, and nobody treats a check-in date as fixed until we all agree one.

Two questions. Would you be willing to check one place for the will, so the search does not rest on A alone? And are you content with the stock of the draft now, or does it still misstate you?
I can look through Dad’s papers at the house. The draft seems fair so far, though I’d like it to keep clear that studio funding matters to me; I can’t give a figure until I’ve worked out the costs.

Closing summary, so all three of you have the same picture.

The list, in each person's own words. You will not subsidize A's purchase and you want a fair financial share. A wants to buy the house with her husband at a family discount, with everyone's agreement, and will not commit in advance to paying full valuation. B wants enough to start a dance studio, cannot give a figure until she has costed it, and says studio funding must stay in plain view. My concerns are that we work from the will rather than memory, and that no plan becomes the front-runner before we know what the will allows.

The corrections I owe you. I wrongly described three separate statements as an agreement, and I have told both your sisters. I also built the draft on a three-way split of the price. You and A both refused to assume that before reading the will, and you were right, so I have struck it. A corrected me as well: she did not know B's reason for wanting money until I passed it on, and I should have left that to B.

Where we stand. Nobody holds the will. A will check your dad's papers and enquire with his solicitor or bank, and B will look through the papers at the house. A is willing to have the house valued. B will cost the studio.

The plan we have not yet agreed. Read the same copy of the will together, get an independent valuation, and let any discount be a specific sum that those giving it up agree to knowingly and in the open. Then weigh the options, including A buying at valuation, against the will and against all six concerns above. Nothing is settled, no shares are assumed, and no check-in date is fixed.

Thank you for raising this. The three of you have done the hard part already: you disagree in the open, and you correct me when I am wrong.
That reflects my position. I’ll wait for the will and valuation before deciding; nothing is agreed yet.
